newsitem.title: IRAQ: Row over observers delays food to Iraqis.
newsitem.headline: Row over observers delays food to Iraqis.

text.p: Wrangling over recruitment and duties of observers could delay the distribution of badly needed food supplies to millions of malnourished Iraqis, diplomatic sources in the Iraqi capital said on Monday.
The observers are to ensure any food shipments reaching Iraq under its oil deal with the United Nations are distributed on an equitable basis. "None of them has arrived so far," one diplomat said.
He said the United States insisted that no purchases from the oil deal, allowing Baghdad sales worth $2 billion in six months, be made unless the 151 international obserbvers are in place.
"The U.N. has no money to recruit them and no country is giving it an advance to go ahead," the diplomat said.
He said it could be sometime before money poured into Iraq's escrow account to pay for the stationing of the observers, their support staff and equipment.
Of the $2 billion Iraq will be left with $1.320 after paying 30 per cent to the victims of its 1990 invasion of Kuwait and other U.N. expenses.

Iraq has been the target of U.N. sanctions, including an oil sales ban, since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. This has crippled the economy and brought ordinary Iraqis untold miseries. The U.N. allowed Iraq the partial sales of oil to alleviate the suffering.
"Time is running out for the ordinary Iraqis bearing the brunt of U.N. trade sanctions. Another month means more deaths and more stunted and malnourished children," said another diplomat.
The U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF said in November that 4,500 Iraqi children died each month from hunger and disease. It put the number of malnourished Iraqis at about four million people.
Iraq has earmarked more than $800 million for food supplies but diplomats said it would be a long time before observers arrived and stocks were built up and then handed out to people.
Iraq resumed partial oil exports under the deal on December 10 and millions of Iraqis are still anxiously waiting for their new rations.
Diplomats also said it was not clear yet whether Iraq and the U.N. had solved all problems concerning logistics and communications once the observers are stationed in the country.
"Negotiations were held at the highest levels and could be still continuing," said one diplomat.
Partial exports by Iraq will allow each Iraqi to receive new rations which U.N. officials say will meet more than two thirds of essential needs.

UNICEF says Iraqi hospitals are in a dire need of life saving medicine and other medical supplies. Reporters taken to Saddam Hospital in Baghdad on Monday saw beds without matresses and blankets and windows without curtains and mothers crying over their emaciated babies.
Some $210 million have been allocated for the purchase of urgently needed medical supplies but these, diplomats said, will not start pouring into the country unless the observers are in place, too.
